about: Data for the chi-square lab (docs/apstat-spec.md section 6). explore.studies are the tables the Explore view opens on; contexts are the Test yourself studies (each makes new tables from its base proportions). design is homogeneity (separate samples or groups: rows are the groups) or independence (one sample, two variables). The model is statistics/assets/tools/math/chi-square-lab.js; every number comes from ApStatDist.
intro: A chi-square test asks whether a two-way table is far from what the null hypothesis predicts. Change any count and watch its expected count, its share of the statistic and the p-value move. The expected counts come from the table's own totals; the statistic adds up how far each cell is from its expected count.
howItWorks:
If $H_0$ is true, each cell's expected count is $\frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}$. Each cell adds $\frac{(O - E)^2}{E}$ to the statistic; the colours show which cells add the most, orange where the observed count is above the expected count and blue where it is below. The sum $\chi^2$ is compared with the $\chi^2$ distribution with $(r - 1)(c - 1)$ degrees of freedom, and the p-value is the area to its right.

  • Homogeneity or independence. The arithmetic is the same. Homogeneity compares the distribution of one variable across separate samples or treatment groups; independence asks whether two variables are associated in one sample.
  • Conditions. Random samples or random assignment, 10% of the population when sampling without replacement, and every expected count at least 5.
  • Chance tables. "Chance table" draws a new table from the null hypothesis itself (each row keeps its total; the counts follow the pooled column proportions), so you can see how big $\chi^2$ gets by chance alone.

Test yourself makes new tables from a seed (the problem code), checks every step against a key the validator recomputes independently, and names the usual slip when an answer misses.

studies.name: Lunch choice at three schools (homogeneity)
studies.story: Random samples of 100 students at each of three schools were asked what they usually eat for lunch.

studies.name: Age and news source (independence)
studies.story: A random sample of 340 adults in a city were asked their age and their main source of news.

studies.name: Fertilizer and flowering (homogeneity, an experiment)
studies.story: A gardener randomly assigned 180 seedlings to two fertilizers, 90 each, and recorded how much each plant flowered.

contexts.story: Separate random samples of students at three schools (North, Central and South) were asked whether they usually eat pizza, salad or a sandwich for lunch. The table on the stage shows the counts.
A random sample of adults in a city were asked their age group and their main source of news. The table on the stage shows the counts.
A gardener randomly assigned seedlings to two fertilizers and recorded how much each plant flowered. The table on the stage shows the counts.
A random sample of households in a town were asked what type of home they live in and whether they own a dog, a cat or no pet. The table on the stage shows the counts.
Separate random samples of downtown and suburban workers were asked how they usually get to work. The table on the stage shows the counts.
